item.title: Manufacturing Happy Hour: 310: The Automation Skills Gap: Why Manufacturers Need to Train the Workforce They Already Have
item.description:
Five years ago, many companies treated training as optional. That’s changing.

Joining Chris is Christelle Keefer, Director of Training and Certification at the Association for Advancing Automation (A3), back for a second visit. Before she started at A3, she spent years at a robotics OEM working with schools, instructors, and customers worldwide. And if she had her way, this conversation would be happening at a punk rock show.

They discuss what automation training should include and what certifications look like for different roles. Christelle also talks about how manufacturers can prepare the existing workforce for new opportunities, and how educators can help students connect with automation.

In this episode, find out:

  • How stackable credentials let working adults build their skills without taking years away from work
  • Why hands-on equipment time and simulation still matter as more training moves online
  • How manufacturers can upskill the workers they already have, and why tying training to a pay increase or promotion matters
  • How colleges work with local employers to shape their programs, and where apprenticeships fit into the picture
  • What A3 is doing to connect students with manufacturing through competitions, mentorship and the Education Pavilion at Automate
  • What Christelle hopes the future of automation will look like, and why she sees a national strategy as part of the picture

Enjoying the show? Please leave us a review here. Even one sentence helps. It’s feedback from Manufacturing All-Stars like you that keeps us going!

Tweetable Quotes:

  • “Nothing beats hands-on training and actually getting your hands onto the software and onto the equipment.” - Christelle Keefer, Director of Training and Certification at the Association for Advancing Automation

item.title: Where Should We Begin? with Esther Perel: I'll Still Be Your Financial Partner, But I'm Done Being Your Wife
item.description:
After a nearly forty-year relationship, they've decided to split. But given the many laws in America that favor married couples, they've decided to try an unconventional arrangement: living 300 miles apart but remaining legally married. They come to Esther wondering how, after decades of emotional enmeshment, they can disentangle their romantic connection while continuing to function like business partners. Esther helps them move into their next phase of life by coaching them past long-held relational patterns so that they can instead offer each other gratitude, regret, and distance.
Producer’s Note: When our anonymous guests do a session with Esther for the podcast, it is an act of generosity for everyone who listens. These sessions are meant not only to support the people in the room with Esther, but all of us who learn from their stories. Our stories have many chapters, and what you hear is just one moment in someone’s journey. So even though the sessions are anonymous, please remember that real people are behind them and they may be reading your comments.
Relationships are undergoing a massive cultural shift. We've never been more connected, and we've never felt more disconnected. We crave understanding and collective experience. We want to be seen but we're optimizing for isolation. Esther believes that the only way to improve our relationships is to remember the basics of being together. This is why she's inviting you to join her for an immersive experience: her international tour, Strangers, Friends, and Lovers. Tickets are selling fast. Get yours now at estherperel.com/tour.
Also, please join me on Entre Nous, my new home on Substack for anyone who wants to live, love, and work with more connection and imagination. I invite you to sign up and become a free or paid member at estherperel.substack.com Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

item.title: This American Life: 901: Is Your Blue My Blue?
item.description:
The doomed project of trying to translate what’s in your head into someone else’s head.

Start a Life Partners free trial to watch our new video, A Night of Stories and Improv.

(00:00:00) Prologue: A while back, Ira woke up with double vision and learned that he had cataracts. After his cataract surgery, he realized the color blue looked very different to him. Now he always wonders: does everyone see the same blue as I do, or is their blue different? (3 minutes)

(00:03:26) Act One: Shaun Bengson has known since he was a kid that he’d very likely lose his hearing as he got older and develop tinnitus. And even after it started, he didn’t do the sensible things that would slow its progression. Shaun and his wife, Abigail, discuss their decisions — and non-decisions — with Ira. And Shaun plays a simulation of what the world now sounds like to him. (27 minutes)

(00:32:50) Act Two: Cluster headaches are sometimes called the most painful medical condition. Researchers who study them wanted to know if that was actually true. They asked cluster patients to compare their headaches to other famously painful conditions. Producer Ike Sriskandarajah, who gets these headaches, was excited to read the findings. But should he tell his pregnant wife? (14 minutes)

(00:46:35) Act Three: Molly’s mom died suddenly last fall, and it flipped the axis of her world. But one day, a friend told her about a special object that really helped him cope with his own father’s death. Molly decides to track this object down. (8 minutes)

item.title: Planet Money: Inside the insurance industry’s destruction lab
item.description:
When you think of someone burning down a house for insurance purposes, you don’t imagine it would ever be the insurance company itself lighting the match. But that’s essentially what’s happening inside a giant destruction laboratory, funded by the insurance industry, in the woods of South Carolina. Scientists and engineers there build household structures — from decks to sheds to single family homes — and subject them to literal trials by fire, hail, and hurricane force wind. It’s all in hopes of determining which building materials and techniques will make communities across the country more resilient to natural disasters and make those natural disasters less expensive for insurance companies. 


Today on the show, Planet Money goes inside the destruction lab to see that high octane experimentation in action and to learn about how the insurance industry has been quietly shaping the world around us for over a century.

item.title: Radiolab: More Perfect: Cruel and Unusual
item.description:
This week, we’re replaying the inaugural episode of More Perfect (first aired in 2016) we explore three little words embedded in the 8th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution: “cruel and unusual.” America has long wrestled with this concept in the context of our strongest punishment, the death penalty. A majority of “we the people” (61 percent, to be exact) are in favor of having it, but inside the Supreme Court, opinions have evolved over time in surprising ways.

And outside of the court, the debate drove one woman in the UK to take on the U.S. death penalty system from Europe. It also caused states to resuscitate old methods used for executing prisoners on death row. And perhaps more than anything, it forced a conversation on what constitutes cruel and unusual punishment.

In this episode, we also include a new conversation with Harvard law professor Carol Steiker and former death-row inmate Damien Nichols about the moment the death penalty finds itself in now. After the botched execution of Christa Pike, and with the government considering livestreaming a firing squad execution, how do we understand the death penalty in 2026?

Special thanks to Claire Phillips, Nina Perry, Stephanie Jenkins, Ralph Dellapiana, Byrd Pinkerton, Elisabeth Semel, Christina Spaulding, Carol Steiker, Damien Nichols, and The Marshall Project

item.title: The Automation Ladies: You Are Either A Risk Or An Investment with Bill Seaman
item.description:
Most manufacturing hiring advice is either vague or completely detached from how industrial automation jobs really work. So I brought on Bill Seaman, Director of People Operations at Philomatic, to get brutally practical about what attracts great engineers, technicians, and field service talent and what quietly drives them away.

We start with the reality a lot of people avoid talking about: layoffs, short tenures, and career pivots. Bill explains how candidates can reframe those moments, show adaptability, and answer the unspoken question every hiring manager has: are you a risk or an investment? From there, we dig into career growth inside OEMs and machine builders, including why companies need strong individual contributor paths (senior and principal roles) instead of forcing great technical people into people management.

Then we get into the hiring mechanics that matter. We break down job descriptions and bias, why bloated “nice-to-have” requirements shrink your applicant pool, and how interview structure can improve both candidate experience and team buy-in. We also cover diversity in manufacturing, visa sponsorship and OPT timelines, and the hidden retention killer many long-tenured companies face: salary compression and outdated pay bands. To round it out, Bill shares benefits that compete when you cannot outspend bigger companies, like real flexibility, schedule options, and creative wellness support.

If you’re hiring in industrial automation or trying to land your next role, you’ll walk away with a clearer playbook. Subscribe, share this with a teammate, and leave us a review with the most outdated hiring rule you want to see disappear.

item.title: NerdWallet's Smart Money Podcast: Read the Fine Print on Dental and Disability Insurance. Plus, Is a Cheaper Home Worth the Distance?
item.description:
Learn how to weigh dental, vision, life and disability coverage, and what a cheaper home far from loved ones could cost.
Is supplemental insurance worth paying for? Hosts Sean Pyles, CFP®, and Elizabeth Ayoola, in the second of our episodes about Open Enrollment season, talk with Victoria Collar, director of knowledge, community and operations at SHRM (the Society for Human Resource Management), about the benefits that often get overlooked: dental, vision, life and disability coverage. They discuss how dental PPOs, DHMOs, indemnity plans and discount plans differ, when bundling dental and vision could save you money, and why waiting periods and annual maximums matter. You’ll also hear why employer-provided life insurance may fall short, how short-term and long-term disability coverage work together, and what hospital indemnity, critical illness and cancer insurance actually pay for.
Then we ask: what does it really cost to live far from your people? Senior news writer Anna Helhoski and NerdWallet mortgage writer Abby Doyle unpack a Federal Reserve study finding that 44% of American families gave or received help with money or caregiving from friends or relatives in the past year. They discuss the hidden costs of buying a cheaper home far from your support network, why many buyers would trade a bigger yard for a walkable neighborhood, how cottage court housing could help people stay close to their communities, and how to weigh connection against affordability in your home search.

item.title: Filmspotting: Direct to Camera, Pt. 1 — Real Life (1979)
item.description:
As co-director of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder is unusually present in front of the camera, arguably overshadowing the film’s ostensible subject, disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. That’s just the start of the film’s unconventionalities, which we’ll get into more next week, but first we’re revisiting a 1979 comedy that predicts Fielder’s turn as the stealth protagonist of his own documentary. As a prototype of the mockumentary form, as well as a satire of the then-nascent genre of reality television, Albert Brooks’ deeply meta debut feature Real Life encourages the audience to recognize an essential fact about documentary filmmaking, which is that cameras inevitably affect the behavior of those in front of it. And this week in Feedback, we correct an oversight in our recent discussion of The Social Network, and touch on some of the other titles we considered for this pairing.
